\paragraph{Neuro-symbolic reasoning.}
We distinguish three paradigms: \emph{specification-generation} \citep{pan2023logiclm, olausson2023linc, ye2024satlm} translates problems into formal specifications before answering; \emph{program-generation} \citep{gao2023pal, chen2023program, lyu2023faithful} produces executable code; both formalize \emph{before} answer generation. \emph{Trace-extraction} (this work) operates post-hoc, inheriting confirmation bias (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}). Recent extensions expand these paradigms with symbolic planning, logic agents, and verified reasoning \citep{ryu2025clover, xu2026dylos, li2025aristotle, wang2025fover, singh2026verge, luo2025logicagent, miya2025eidoku}; \citet{amonkar2025realitycheck} show formalization quality degrades with problem complexity; \citet{chan2026position} argue logical soundness alone is unreliable for neurosymbolic verification. Prior studies \citep{olausson2023linc, amonkar2025realitycheck} note high formalization error rates but treat them as quality problems; we show the errors are \emph{systematically biased} toward the model's answer. Observation~1 establishes that self-extracted constraints reduce SICA to majority vote under degeneration ($C \approx\!\!\perp Y \mid A$; Figure~\ref{fig:causal-dag}), making self-verification an information bottleneck. \citet{huang2024selfcorrect} show LLMs cannot self-correct without external feedback; our findings extend this limitation to formal self-verification, showing that even Z3-validated constraints carry no information beyond majority voting.

1	Can symbolic verification via a provably sound solver improve Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning when constraints are self-extracted from the model's own traces? We find no evidence of improvement. We introduce Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts logical constraints from chain-of-thought traces and selects answers via weighted MAX-SAT. Despite Z3 validating 99\% of self-extracted constraints, SICA produces answers identical to majority voting on over 90\% of problems across six models (7B--32B) and three reasoning domains. No condition shows a significant positive effect after FDR control; four of six powered conditions confirm equivalence within $\pm$2\,pp (TOST), though ten conditions remain underpowered for effects below ${\sim}$2\,pp. We systematically diagnose the failure as \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: self-extracted constraints track the model's majority answer (bias ratios $1.66$--$4.97\times$ across nine models, 7B to frontier). We identify the structural mechanism---under source-attribution scoring and empirical degeneration, SICA reduces to majority vote (Observation~1)---and the $M{\to}T{\to}A{\to}C$ Markov chain that bounds self-extracted information (Remark~1), advancing beyond \citet{huang2024selfcorrect}'s findings to formal self-verification. Twenty-seven training-free variants within the constraint-extraction paradigm fail due to a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off. Preliminary cross-architecture verification escapes the bias ($+6.67$\,pp on the weakest generator, $p < 0.001$). Three zero-cost diagnostics characterize failure modes across all 60 tested conditions within this paradigm.

\looseness=-1 Figure~\ref{fig:regime-scatter} reveals the regime structure underlying these results. Fleiss' $\kappa$ ranges from 0.21 to 0.82 across conditions, yielding $K_{\text{eff}} = 1.20\text{--}3.62$ at $K = 12$ (Table~\ref{tab:independence}, Appendix). Positive $\Delta$ requires both sufficient $K_{\text{eff}}$ ($\leq 1.30$ never improves) and reasonable SC accuracy ($K_{\text{eff}} = 3.62$ with SC $= 39\%$ degrades rather than helps). Three regimes emerge: Type~C (SC $\leq 40\%$), where low base accuracy causes error amplification; an intermediate band (50--60\%), containing the only positive trends; and Type~A (SC $\geq 60\%$), where symbolic confirmation bias dominates. Seed-level noise is substantial: across three Mistral-7B seeds, $\kappa \in [0.41, 0.51]$ yet $\Delta$ ranges from $+2.94$ to $-2.45$\,pp, indicating that constraint quality varies beyond what independence alone predicts. We trace the failure mechanism in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.

\looseness=-1 TOST equivalence tests \citep{lakens2017equivalence} with pre-registered margin $\pm 2$\,pp---based on the smallest meaningful SC gain reported in \citet{wang2023sc}---confirm four conditions as equivalent; ten remain underpowered for effects below ${\sim}2$\,pp (MDE 1.86--4.84\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:power}). Four-seed replication on Qwen2.5-14B $\times$ FOLIO confirms the pattern ($\Delta \in [0.00, -2.01]$\,pp).

lines: We test this intuition through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts logical constraints from reasoning traces (prompted as first-order logic; 99\% are propositional at the Z3 level) and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}). The result is unequivocal: despite Z3 validating nearly all self-extracted constraints, SICA produces answers identical to majority voting on the vast majority of problems. Across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains, and multi-seed replication, no condition shows a significant positive effect after FDR control (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}). Four conditions confirm equivalence within $\pm$2\,pp; ten remain underpowered for effects below ${\sim}$2\,pp.

-The failure is not in the solver but in the constraints it operates on. Self-extracted constraints systematically support the model's majority answer, a phenomenon we term \emph{symbolic confirmation bias} (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}). Because each trace determines both an answer and its constraints, the formal channel reduces to a weighted echo of the majority vote. We prove this degeneration is structural (Observation~1) and show it holds across nine models from 7B to frontier scale. Prior work shows LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning without external feedback \citep{huang2024selfcorrect}; our formal analysis advances beyond \citet{huang2024selfcorrect}'s empirical findings, providing structural formalization and actionable diagnostics for self-verification.

Prior work shows LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning without external feedback \citep{huang2024selfcorrect}; our formal analysis extends and formalizes \citet{huang2024selfcorrect}'s empirical findings, providing structural formalization and actionable diagnostics for self-verification.

Twenty-seven training-free variants within the constraint-extraction paradigm confirm the trade-off is fundamental (\S\ref{sec:remediation}): methods that break trace correlation destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy fail to achieve independence. Cross-architecture verification provides preliminary evidence of escape: a structurally independent verifier yields significant gains when it exceeds the generator's accuracy, with benefit governed by a capability-gap pattern between verifier and generator (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}). Three zero-cost diagnostics enable practitioners to predict a priori whether any self-extraction-based aggregation method will help (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic-framework}).

On Mistral-7B FOLIO, when SICA errs, 83.3\% of constraints support the incorrect answer---bias ratio $4.97\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model-bias})---and 94\% of errors overlap with SC. Z3 rejects only 3.4\% of constraints, and MAX-SAT produces answers identical to count-only aggregation on $\geq$99\% of problems across all weight settings $\alpha$ (Table~\ref{tab:alpha-ablation}), confirming that the formal verification layer is vacuous (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}): 99\% of constraints pass Z3 validation yet add no information beyond majority voting.

+\looseness=-1 Self-extracted constraints systematically align with the model's majority answer---a structural limitation of self-extraction pipelines, not a cognitive bias analogy. On Mistral-7B FOLIO, when SICA errs, 83.3\% of constraints support the incorrect answer---bias ratio $4.97\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model-bias})---and 94\% of errors overlap with SC. Z3 rejects only 3.4\% of constraints, and MAX-SAT produces answers identical to count-only aggregation on $\geq$99\% of problems across all weight settings $\alpha$ (Table~\ref{tab:alpha-ablation}), confirming that the formal verification layer is vacuous (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}): 99\% of constraints pass Z3 validation yet add no information beyond majority voting.

\looseness=-1 Empirically, confirmation bias extends beyond incorrect instances. On problems where SC selects the correct answer, constraints still disproportionately support the majority ($\text{BR}_\text{correct}$ $1.29$--$3.64\times$ across all six tested conditions, with 5/6 showing $\text{BR}_\text{correct} \geq \text{BR}_\text{wrong}$), confirming that self-extracted constraints track distributional frequency rather than logical validity. A permutation null model---randomizing constraint--answer associations while preserving per-trace counts (1{,}000 permutations)---yields $\text{BR}_\text{null} \approx \text{BR}_\text{obs}$ ($\text{BR}_\text{excess} \approx 0$; $p > 0.7$) across all tested conditions, confirming that BR quantifies the degree of extraction degeneration---how completely constraints collapse to majority-vote equivalents---rather than an independent bias signal. The bias is inherent to the majority-vote geometry (Observation~1): under source-attribution scoring, BR $> 1$ follows from trace-count distributions, not extraction artifacts.
